## Generalized PIPE Design with Epsilon-Tapering for Dose-Finding Studies

The gPIPE package implements the Product of Independent beta Probabilities Escalation (PIPE) design for drug-combination dose-finding trials, for any number of drugs.
It covers the original PIPE design for the maximum tolerated dose contour of Mander and Sweeting (2015) and PIPE with epsilon-tapering for the minimum effective dose of Cheung, Chandereng and Diaz (2022).
The estimate is found exactly by a minimum cut on the partial order of the dose combinations, and whole trials can be simulated to give operating characteristics.

## Installation

You can install the development version of gPIPE from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("xlai/gPIPE")
```

## Example

Here's a basic example of setting up a dose-finding trial using gPIPE:

```{r example, eval=FALSE}
library(gPIPE)

# 4 x 4 grid of two drugs, Mander & Sweeting design for the MTD
grid <- DoseGrid(levels = c(A = 4, B = 4))
design <- ms_design(grid, theta = 0.2, prior_median = 0.2, prior_strength = 1 / 16, N = 50)

# Estimate and next dose from the data so far (one row per patient)
data <- data.frame(A = c(1, 1, 2), B = c(1, 2, 2), y = c(0, 0, 1))
estimate(design, data)
next_dose(design, data)

# Simulate 1000 trials under a true toxicity scenario
truth <- outer(c(0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16), c(0, 0.06, 0.12, 0.18), `+`)
sim <- simulate(design, nsim = 1000, seed = 1, truth = truth)
```

## Features

- Implementation of the generalized PIPE design for dose-finding studies
- Support for epsilon-tapering to improve dose-space exploration
- Flexible admissibility rules for dose combinations
- Multiple dose selection strategies
- Simulation tools for design calibration and evaluation
